How Reliable Is Individualized Functional-Network Attribution in Resting-State fMRI Cognitive Prediction in ADNI?

A Scan–Rescan Evaluation
\fnameSheethal \lnameBhat \authorsEmailsheethal.bhat@fau.de Martensstr. \housenumber3 \zipcode91058 Erlangen Germany \isResponsibleAuthor Affiliation: Pattern Recognition Lab, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU)    \fnameMahfuzur Rahman \lnameChowdhury Martensstr. \housenumber3 \zipcode91058 Erlangen Germany Affiliation: Pattern Recognition Lab, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU)    \fnameImam Ahmed \lnameShaik \authorsEmailimamahmed.shaik@siemens-healthineers.com Henkestr. \housenumber127 \zipcode91052 Erlangen Germany Affiliation: Siemens Healthineers    \fnameRose Dawn \lnameBharat \authorsEmaildrrosedawnbharat@gmail.com Martensstr. \housenumber3 \zipcode91058 Erlangen Germany Affiliation: Pattern Recognition Lab, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU)    \fnameSiming \lnameBayer Martensstr. \housenumber3 \zipcode91058 Erlangen Germany Affiliation: Pattern Recognition Lab, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU)    \fnameAndreas \lnameMaier \authorsEmailandreas.maier@fau.de Martensstr. \housenumber3 \zipcode91058 Erlangen Germany Affiliation: Pattern Recognition Lab, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) Email: sheethal.bhat@fau.de Affiliation: 1Pattern Recognition Lab, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), Martensstr. 3, 91058 Erlangen, Germany
2Siemens Healthineers, Henkestr. 127, 91052 Erlangen, Germany
Abstract

Individualized attribution estimates which functional networks drive a model prediction for a given subject and is often proposed as an interpretable resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) biomarker, but its test–retest reliability is rarely quantified. We evaluate per-subject network-ablation attribution for a frozen resting-state functional connectivity (FC) predictor (Schaefer-200 FC predicting MMSE/ADAS-Cog13) trained on N=875N{=}875 subjects from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), using (i) within-session split-half, (ii) scan–rescan repeat visits (74 subjects, 205 baseline–repeat pairs; median inter-visit interval 24.4 months), and (iii) a subject-level permutation null. Split-half reliability is near-ceiling (Spearman ρ=0.948\rho{=}0.948/0.9500.950) but drops on scan–rescan (ρ=0.609\rho{=}0.609/0.6160.616). Under the mismatched-subject null, correlations remain substantial (ρ≈0.46\rho{\approx}0.46–0.470.47), indicating strong population-shared structure, yet matched pairs exceed this null (z≈6.6z{\approx}6.6–6.96.9, p≤10−4p\leq 10^{-4}). Thus, in ADNI, individualized network attribution contains a modest but non-zero person-specific component atop a strong population-shared pattern. We recommend reporting scan–rescan reliability together with a permutation-null control, rather than within-session proxies alone, to avoid overstating individual specificity.

1 Introduction

Models that map resting-state functional connectivity (FC) to cognition and clinical phenotypes are increasingly used in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) neuroimaging [4, 16]. Beyond group-level accuracy, a common objective is individualized attribution: for a given subject, estimating which functional networks drive that subject’s prediction. Such per-subject attribution is only meaningful if it is reproducible.

Reliability is a central constraint. Large-scale analyses suggest that stable brain–behavior effects often require much larger samples than historically used [11], and FC test–retest reliability is frequently modest (pooled mean edge-level Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, ICC ≈0.29\approx 0.29) [13]. The ICC describes how reproducibly a single connectivity edge is measured. Prior work on subject-specific parcellations reports reproducibility across short-interval repeat sessions [17, 10], but does not quantify test–retest reliability of model-derived attribution signatures over the multi-year intervals typical of aging cohorts.

An additional aspect is attribution stability: feature-importance maps can vary substantially under resampling, noise, and other perturbations even when predictive accuracy is similar [1, 7]. In FC prediction, however, attribution work has largely emphasized group-averaged importance. For connectomes rather than attributions, differential identifiability formalizes the person-specific, test–retest-identifiable component [2], and permutation-null models are standard for separating population-shared from person-specific structure [5, 12]. Neither has been applied to per-subject attribution signatures. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work combines per-subject attribution of an FC-based cognitive predictor with a quantitative test–retest evaluation on independent repeat scans of the same individuals.

We address this gap using a frozen FC-based multilayer perceptron (FC-MLP) trained to jointly predict MMSE and ADAS-Cog13 from Schaefer-200 FC on N=875N{=}875 ADNI subjects (Sect. 2). Instead of edge-level ICC, we assess test–retest consistency of each subject’s network-attribution ranking. We compute per-subject network-ablation signatures and evaluate reproducibility with three checks: within-session split-half, scan–rescan across independent repeat visits, and a cluster-aware subject-level permutation null. The main contributions in this study are:

  1. 1.

    Quantify how split-half overestimates scan–rescan reliability of per-subject network attribution (74 subjects; 205 session pairs).

  2. 2.

    Use a subject-level permutation null to estimate the mismatched-subject baseline and the residual person-specific component.

  3. 3.

    Provide reporting recommendations to avoid overstating individual specificity.

2 Methods

To attribute a prediction to functional networks for a single subject, let ff denote the frozen FC-MLP mapping a subject’s connectivity vector xx to a two-dimensional prediction 𝐲^=f⁡(x)\hat{\mathbf{y}}=f(x) with targets t∈{MMSE,ADAS-Cog13}t\in\{\text{MMSE},\text{ADAS-Cog13}\}. For a given target tt, we write the scalar prediction as y^(t)=[f⁡(x)]t\hat{y}^{(t)}=[f(x)]_{t}.

For each of the seven Yeo networks [18] n∈{n\in\{Vis, SomMot, DorsAttn, SalVentAttn, Limbic, Cont, Default}\} (see Fig. 1), we ablate the input by zeroing all FC edges incident to nodes in nn. Because the model input concatenates an FC vector and an edge-coverage mask, x=[FC;mask]x=[\mathrm{FC};\mathrm{mask}], we apply the ablation to both operands: the ablated edges are set to zero in the FC vector and their corresponding mask entries are also set to zero. This yields x∖nx_{\setminus n} and y^n(t)=[f⁡(x∖n)]t\hat{y}^{(t)}_{n}=[f(x_{\setminus n})]_{t}. The per-target network importance is then In(t)=y^(t)−y^n(t)I^{(t)}_{n}=\hat{y}^{(t)}-\hat{y}^{(t)}_{n}, and the subject-specific importance signature for target tt is 𝐈(t)=(I1(t),…,I7(t))\mathbf{I}^{(t)}=(I^{(t)}_{1},\ldots,I^{(t)}_{7}).

This implementation reproduces the group-level ablation results (Fig. 1) for all 7 × 2 network–target combinations to six decimal places. Attribution reliability between two occasions a,ba,b for the same subject is the Spearman rank correlation ρ⁡(𝐈a,𝐈b)\rho(\mathbf{I}_{a},\mathbf{I}_{b}), i.e., the agreement in the within-subject network ranking.

Fig. 2 summarizes three reliability checks. (i) Split-half: for each test subject (n=132n{=}132), we split the denoised rs-fMRI time series after scrubbing into odd/even surviving volumes, recompute FC and attribution per half, and compute ρ⁡(𝐈half-A,𝐈half-B)\rho(\mathbf{I}_{\text{half-A}},\mathbf{I}_{\text{half-B}}) (minimum 30 volumes per half; 0 exclusions). We additionally test whether split-half ρ\rho increases with per-half scan duration. (ii) Scan–rescan: we attribute independent repeat-visit rs-fMRI and compute ρ⁡(𝐈baseline,𝐈repeat)\rho(\mathbf{I}_{\text{baseline}},\mathbf{I}_{\text{repeat}}) for baseline ×\times all follow-ups, yielding 205 pairs from 74 subjects with uneven repeats (ki∈[1,12]k_{i}\in[1,12]; 30 subjects contribute 1 pair, 18 contribute 2, 13 contribute 3; tail to 12). (iii) Permutation null: for B=10,000B{=}10{,}000 permutations, we draw a derangement π\pi of the 74 subjects, pair each subject ii’s baseline signature with the repeat signatures of subject π⁡(i)\pi(i) (repeats kept as a block), and recompute the subject-level mean reliability. With TobsT_{\mathrm{obs}} the observed subject-level mean and bb the number of permutations with statistic ≥Tobs\geq T_{\mathrm{obs}}, we report p=(b+1)/(B+1)p=(b+1)/(B+1) and z=(Tobs−μnull)/σnullz=(T_{\mathrm{obs}}-\mu_{\mathrm{null}})/\sigma_{\mathrm{null}} [12].

Artifact checks

Edge-count: let c∈ℝ7c\in\mathbb{R}^{7} be the fixed vector of ablated edge counts (unique edges zeroed when ablating each network). For each subject we compute the across-network Spearman correlation ρ⁡(𝐈(t),c)\rho(\mathbf{I}^{(t)},c) (7 items) and summarize it across subjects by its mean, separately per target; with only 7 items, Spearman ρ\rho is highly discrete, so this check is treated as descriptive. For scan–rescan, we first average each subject’s per-pair ρ⁡(𝐈(t),c)\rho(\mathbf{I}^{(t)},c) across that subject’s repeat visits and then compute the across-subject mean. Scan duration: we correlate (Spearman, across the 132 test subjects) each subject’s per-half scan duration (seconds; half A, equivalent to half B up to one volume) with split-half ρ\rho.

Aggregation and inference

All Spearman correlations are computed separately within each of the three trained runs and averaged across runs. Spearman ρ\rho uses average ranks for ties; no ties occurred in any importance signature (verified for all 1,674 scan–rescan signatures, i.e., 279 sessions ×\times 2 targets ×\times 3 runs, and all split-half signatures). As subjects contribute unequal numbers of repeat pairs, scan–rescan is summarized at the subject level by first averaging each subject’s per-pair ρ\rho values and then summarizing across subjects; we also report the pair-pooled mean for comparability. Uncertainty on headline scan–rescan and split-half means is a 95 % percentile bootstrap CI over 10,000 resamples of subjects (resampling whole subjects). We test the split-half versus scan–rescan gap with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test across the 74 subjects present in both analyses.

3 Experimental details

3.1 Data description

ADNI is a multi-site, longitudinal study of aging and Alzheimer’s disease with multimodal neuroimaging [9]. We analyzed data from N=875N{=}875 unique ADNI participants who had both T1-weighted MRI and rs-fMRI scans. Within the N=875N{=}875 cohort, diagnoses are CN (n=464n{=}464), MCI (n=315n{=}315), Dementia (n=94n{=}94), and unknown (n=2n{=}2). Age is 72.6±7.972.6\pm 7.9 years (range 50–97); 489 subjects are female and 386 male. Subjects were enrolled in ADNI1 (n=37n{=}37), ADNI-GO (n=38n{=}38), ADNI2 (n=256n{=}256), ADNI3 (n=474n{=}474), and ADNI4 (n=68n{=}68); 2 unknown. rs-fMRI scans were acquired at 3.0 T across 53 sites with heterogeneous protocols (TR 0.607–6.02 s; 96–972 volumes after removal of initial volumes). For the upstream prediction model, the cohort is split once at the subject level into fixed train/validation/test partitions of 611/132/132 stratified by diagnosis. We evaluate attribution and reliability only on the held-out 132-subject test split; scan–rescan further restricts to test subjects with repeat-visit rs-fMRI.

3.2 Implementation details

We analyze a trained FC-MLP and keep its weights fixed for all attribution and reliability analyses.

Input features

rs-fMRI preprocessing includes motion correction, HD-BET brain extraction [8], rigid rs-fMRI→\toT1 registration, detrending, and nuisance regression of mean white-matter (WM) and cerebrospinal-fluid (CSF) signals plus 5 anatomical CompCor (aCompCor) components [3] from a combined WM/CSF mask, without global signal regression. Time series are band-pass filtered (0.01–0.1 Hz, using each subject’s TR), zz-scored, and scrubbed at framewise displacement (FD) >0.5>0.5 mm after filtering; FD was computed from translation magnitude only rather than the full six-parameter formulation [14], as rotation parameters were not retained upstream. No spatial smoothing or slice-timing correction is applied. We compute Schaefer-200 [15] FC as a Fisher-zz transformed 200×200200\times 200 Pearson correlation matrix and vectorize the upper triangle (19,900 edges). An edge-coverage mask is concatenated, yielding a 39,800-dimensional input.

Model and training (frozen)

The FC-MLP encoder maps 39,800→256→12839{,}800\to 256\to 128 with LayerNorm/GELU/dropout (0.3), and the decoder maps 128→64→2128\to 64\to 2 with GELU/dropout (0.3). The model is trained with Huber loss (δ=1.0\delta{=}1.0) using Adam (lr=10−4\mathrm{lr}=10^{-4}, weight decay 10−510^{-5}; no schedule/warmup), batch size 16, and up to 100 epochs. Early stopping uses patience 15 on validation loss; we keep the single best checkpoint (lowest validation loss). During training only, an augmentation zeros 5 randomly chosen parcels per sample. Targets are zz-scored on train only and inverse-transformed for reporting. Three independent runs with different random initializations share the same fixed split. ComBat harmonization [6] uses the TR group as batch variable (a proxy for acquisition protocol) and protects diagnosis, whose composition differs across TR groups (χ2=35.66\chi^{2}{=}35.66, p<0.001p<0.001); no other covariates are included. It is fit on the training split only, never refit, and applied to validation/test subjects and split-half halves, but not to repeat-visit sessions (both sides of scan–rescan use pre-ComBat features).

3.3 Results

The frozen predictor is weak: on the n=113n{=}113 test subjects with both targets, R2=0.053±0.034R^{2}{=}0.053\pm 0.034 for MMSE and 0.087±0.0370.087\pm 0.037 for ADAS-Cog13 (mean ±\pm SD over runs). As a diagnostic check, the predicted ADAS-Cog13 score separates CN from Dementia with AUC 0.7800.780 (95 % bootstrap CI 0.611–0.911; n=72n=72 of the 113 subjects with both targets: 58 CN, 14 Dementia).

Within-session split-half reliability is near-ceiling for both targets (mean ρ=0.948\rho{=}0.948/0.9500.950, median ≈0.99\approx 0.99; Tab. 1). On independent repeat visits (205 session pairs from 74 subjects), subject-level scan–rescan reliability drops to ρ=0.609\rho{=}0.609 (MMSE) and 0.6160.616 (ADAS-Cog13), with large between-subject variation (10th–90th percentiles 0.340.34–0.900.90 and 0.330.33–0.850.85). Pair-pooled means are slightly lower (0.5930.593/0.5880.588) because subjects with more follow-ups receive more weight. Restricted to the same 74 subjects, split-half reliability is 0.9330.933/0.9390.939, a paired difference of 0.3240.324/0.3230.323 (Wilcoxon p<10−12p<10^{-12}), indicating that split-half substantially overestimates test–retest reliability.

Under the subject-level permutation null, mismatched subjects still correlate strongly (ρ=0.463\rho{=}0.463/0.4720.472), but the matched statistic exceeds the null (z=6.89z{=}6.89/6.636.63; p≤10−4p\leq 10^{-4}), corresponding to a modest person-specific excess of ≈0.15\approx 0.15 (MMSE) and ≈0.14\approx 0.14 (ADAS-Cog13). The artifact checks do not indicate a network-size effect: mean edge-count correlations ρ⁡(𝐈(t),c)\rho(\mathbf{I}^{(t)},c) are weakly negative for split-half (MMSE −0.120-0.120; ADAS-Cog13 −0.163-0.163) and repeat visits (MMSE −0.112-0.112; ADAS-Cog13 −0.158-0.158). Split-half reliability increases with per-half scan duration (ρ=0.199\rho{=}0.199/0.2770.277), consistent with sampling-noise limits, although duration is confounded with acquisition protocol in ADNI.

4 Discussion

Per-subject attribution reliability depends strongly on protocol: split-half is near-ceiling (ρ≈0.95\rho{\approx}0.95), but drops on scan–rescan across independent repeat visits (ρ≈0.61\rho{\approx}0.61–0.620.62), consistent with additional between-visit variability beyond within-session sampling noise. The permutation null suggests that much of this structure is population-shared, with only a modest person-specific excess; robustness to other cohorts, preprocessing, parcellations, attribution operators, and models remains untested.

The coexistence of shared and person-specific structure mirrors FC itself, where connectomes are identifiable across sessions [5, 2] yet test–retest reliability is modest [13]. The strong shared profile likely has two sources. First, the ablations overlap by construction: every between-network edge (i,j)(i,j) with i∈ni\in n, j∈mj\in m is zeroed in both x∖nx_{\setminus n} and x∖mx_{\setminus m}, coupling In(t)I^{(t)}_{n} and Im(t)I^{(t)}_{m}; within-network-only ablation would remove this overlap. Second, the weak predictor may respond mainly to group-level FC structure. Because ρ\rho is bounded above, a high shared baseline leaves little room for an individual excess, so the person-specific component may be underestimated.

Limitations include the modest repeat-visit sample (74 subjects; 205 session pairs) and the weak, run-variable predictor (Sect. 3). Repeat-visit sessions were not ComBat-harmonized, so part of the split-half to scan–rescan gap may reflect this mismatch. Inter-visit intervals are long and variable (median 24.4 months, IQR 12.2–48.4) and are not modeled.

We therefore recommend treating within-session proxies as expected upper bounds, reporting scan–rescan estimates when repeat visits exist, and including a permutation-null (or equivalent) control; these recommendations should be validated in further aging/AD cohorts such as OASIS-3 and AIBL. In summary, per-subject network attributions are far less reproducible across visits than within-session estimates suggest, and most of their apparent stability reflects a pattern shared across the cohort, so individual specificity should be demonstrated against an explicit population baseline before attributions are interpreted as personal biomarkers.
